items.title: A portfolio's return
items.prose: A portfolio holds weights $\mathbf{w} = (0.5, 0.3, 0.2)$ in three assets. This month the assets return $\mathbf{r} = (4\%, -2\%, 10\%)$.
items.question: What is the portfolio's return, $\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{r}$?

feedback.generic: Multiply each return by its weight, then add the three products.

byKey.average: You took the plain average of the returns. Each return counts in proportion to its weight.
byKey.sum: You added the returns without their weights.

explain.text: $\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{r} = 0.5 \times 4\% + 0.3 \times (-2\%) + 0.2 \times 10\% = 2\% - 0.6\% + 2\% = 3.4\%$. The weights add to 1, so this is a weighted average.

items.title: Elimination step by step
items.prose: Eliminate $$\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 & 3 \\ -2 & 1 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$$ to upper triangular form, with no row swaps. $\ell_{ij}$ is the multiplier that clears row $i$, column $j$.
items.question: Fill in the three multipliers and the third pivot.

feedback.correct: Pivots 2, 1 and 3, with multipliers 2, $-1$ and 2.
feedback.generic: Each multiplier is the entry to clear over the current pivot, using the rows as they stand now.

explain.text: $R_2 - 2R_1$ gives $(0, 1, 1)$ and $R_3 + R_1$ gives $(0, 2, 5)$, so $\ell_{21} = 2$ and $\ell_{31} = -1$. Then $\ell_{32} = \tfrac{2}{1} = 2$, and $R_3 - 2R_2$ gives $(0, 0, 3)$. The third pivot is 3.

items.title: A perpendicular vector
items.prose: Take $\mathbf{u} = (1, 2, -1)$.
items.question: Which vector is orthogonal to $\mathbf{u}$?

options.why: That is $2\mathbf{u}$, parallel to it. Its dot product with $\mathbf{u}$ is 12.
You flipped the middle sign. The dot product is $1 - 4 - 1 = -4$.
That is $-\mathbf{u}$. Opposite is not perpendicular: the dot product is $-6$.

feedback.generic: Orthogonal means the dot product is 0. Test each option.

explain.text: $\mathbf{u} \cdot (1, 0, 1) = 1 + 0 - 1 = 0$, so they are orthogonal. The other three have dot products 12, $-4$ and $-6$.

items.title: Arrows that only stretch
items.prose: The matrix is $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$.
items.question: Tap every arrow that is an eigenvector of $\mathbf{A}$.

feedback.correct: $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{e}$ stretch by 4, and $\mathbf{b}$ by 1.
feedback.generic: Work out $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}$ for each arrow. It counts when the image is a multiple of $\mathbf{v}$.

byKey.no-flip: You left out $\mathbf{e}$. It points away from $\mathbf{a}$, but $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{e} = (-4, -4) = 4\mathbf{e}$.
byKey.no-one: You left out $\mathbf{b}$. $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{b} = (-1, 2) = \mathbf{b}$, and a stretch by 1 still counts.
byKey.c: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{c} = (5, 2)$, which is not a multiple of $(2, -1)$. The arrow turns.
byKey.d: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{d} = (-5, -2)$, which is not a multiple of $(-2, 1)$. The arrow turns.

explain.text: $\det(\mathbf{A} - \lambda\mathbf{I}) = \lambda^2 - 5\lambda + 4$, so the eigenvalues are 4 and 1. The line through $(1, 1)$ stretches by 4 and holds $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{e}$. The line through $(-1, 2)$ is left as it is, so $\mathbf{b}$ counts too.

items.title: A quarter turn
items.prose: A matrix turns the whole plane a quarter turn anticlockwise about the origin.
items.question: Which matrix is it?

options.why: You wrote the images of $\mathbf{e}_1$ and $\mathbf{e}_2$ as rows. That matrix turns clockwise.
That is a half turn: it sends every arrow to its opposite.
That swaps the coordinates: a reflection in the line $y = x$.

feedback.correct: $\mathbf{e}_1$ lands on $(0, 1)$ and $\mathbf{e}_2$ on $(-1, 0)$: those are the columns.
feedback.generic: Find where $\mathbf{e}_1$ and $\mathbf{e}_2$ land, and write each image as a column.

explain.text: A quarter turn anticlockwise sends $\mathbf{e}_1 = (1, 0)$ to $(0, 1)$ and $\mathbf{e}_2 = (0, 1)$ to $(-1, 0)$. Column $j$ is the image of $\mathbf{e}_j$. This is $\mathbf{R}(90°)$.

items.title: Counting free directions
items.prose: $\mathbf{A}$ is a $3 \times 5$ matrix of rank 3.
items.question: What is the dimension of its nullspace $N(\mathbf{A})$?

options.why: You subtracted the rank from the number of rows. $r + \dim N(\mathbf{A}) = n$ counts columns.
You gave the rank. The nullspace takes the columns without pivots.
You counted every column. Three of them have pivots.

feedback.correct: Five columns, three with pivots, so two free variables.
feedback.generic: Use $r + \dim N(\mathbf{A}) = n$, where $n$ is the number of columns.

explain.text: $\mathbf{A}$ has $n = 5$ columns and $r = 3$ pivots. The other two columns give free variables, one special solution each. So $\dim N(\mathbf{A}) = 5 - 3 = 2$.

items.title: The closest point on a line
items.prose: The line runs through the origin along $\mathbf{a} = (2, 1)$. The point $\mathbf{b} = (1, 5)$ is off it. P rides the line.
items.question: Drag P to the projection of $\mathbf{b}$ onto the line.

feedback.correct: $\mathbf{p} = \tfrac{7}{5}(2, 1) = (2.8, 1.4)$, where the dashed segment meets the line at a right angle.
feedback.generic: Use $\mathbf{p} = \dfrac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a}}\mathbf{a}$, or slide P until the distance is smallest.

byKey.below: You dropped straight down from $\mathbf{b}$. The shortest path meets the slanted line at a right angle.
byKey.tip: You stopped at the head of $\mathbf{a}$. The projection is a multiple of $\mathbf{a}$, here $1.4\mathbf{a}$.
byKey.P: Not at the closest point yet. Watch the caption and stop where the distance is smallest.

explain.text: $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 7$ and $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a} = 5$, so $\mathbf{p} = 1.4\,\mathbf{a} = (2.8, 1.4)$. The error $\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{p} = (-1.8, 3.6)$ has dot product 0 with $\mathbf{a}$. Every other point of the line is further away.

items.title: The characteristic polynomial
items.prose: Take $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$. Write $x$ in place of $\lambda$.
items.question: Write $\det(\mathbf{A} - x\mathbf{I})$ as a polynomial in $x$.

feedback.correct: $(1 - x)(2 - x) - 6 = x^2 - 3x - 4$, so the eigenvalues are 4 and $-1$.
feedback.generic: Subtract $x$ down the diagonal, then take $ad - bc$.

byKey.plus-bc: You added $bc = 6$. The determinant subtracts it.
byKey.trace-sign: Your $x$ term has the wrong sign. It is $-(\text{trace})\,x = -3x$.

explain.text: $\det\begin{pmatrix} 1 - x & 2 \\ 3 & 2 - x \end{pmatrix} = (1 - x)(2 - x) - 6 = x^2 - 3x - 4$. Its roots 4 and $-1$ add to the trace 3 and multiply to $\det\mathbf{A} = -4$.

items.title: Shear first, then turn
items.prose: $\mathbf{S} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ is a shear and $\mathbf{R} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ a quarter turn. You apply $\mathbf{S}$ first, then $\mathbf{R}$.
items.question: Which single matrix does both?

options.why: That is $\mathbf{SR}$: you wrote the first move first. The first move sits on the right.
You added $\mathbf{R} + \mathbf{S}$. Doing one move after another multiplies.
You multiplied entry by entry. Each entry of a product is a row dotted with a column.

feedback.correct: $\mathbf{RS}$: entry $(i, j)$ is row $i$ of $\mathbf{R}$ dotted with column $j$ of $\mathbf{S}$.
feedback.generic: Applying $\mathbf{S}$ then $\mathbf{R}$ to $\mathbf{x}$ gives $\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x}) = (\mathbf{RS})\mathbf{x}$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{RS} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, while $\mathbf{SR} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. The two orders differ. The move done first stands next to $\mathbf{x}$.

items.title: How much area grows
items.prose: The matrix $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$ sends the unit square to the shaded parallelogram.
items.question: What is the area of the parallelogram?

feedback.correct: $\det\mathbf{A} = 3 \times 4 - 1 \times 2 = 10$, and the square had area 1.
feedback.generic: The area scale is $|\det\mathbf{A}| = |ad - bc|$.

byKey.added: You added $bc$. The determinant subtracts it: $ad - bc$.
byKey.diagonal: You multiplied the diagonal only. Subtract $bc = 2$.

explain.text: Every area is multiplied by $|\det\mathbf{A}| = |12 - 2| = 10$. The unit square has area 1, so its image has area 10.

items.title: A stock's beta
items.prose: Five days of returns, in %: the market $\mathbf{m} = (-1, 0, 1, 2, 3)$ and a stock $\mathbf{s} = (-2, 0, 1, 3, 3)$. Fit $s = \alpha + \beta m$ by least squares.
items.question: What is $\hat\beta$?

feedback.correct: Centred cross-products 13 over centred squares 10.
feedback.generic: Use $\hat\beta = \dfrac{\sum (m_i - \bar m)(s_i - \bar s)}{\sum (m_i - \bar m)^2}$, or the normal equations with a column of ones.

byKey.no-intercept: You dropped the column of ones, forcing the line through the origin: $\tfrac{\mathbf{m} \cdot \mathbf{s}}{\mathbf{m} \cdot \mathbf{m}} = 1.2$.
byKey.reversed: You fitted the market on the stock and inverted the slope. Least squares measures vertical gaps.
byKey.ends: You joined the first and last points. Least squares uses every point.

explain.text: $\bar m = 1$ and $\bar s = 1$. The centred cross-products add to 13 and the centred squares to 10. So $\hat\beta = 1.3$ and $\hat\alpha = 1 - 1.3 = -0.3$.

items.title: Bowls that only curve up
items.prose: Four symmetric matrices.
items.question: Which are positive definite? Select all that apply.

options.why: You trusted the positive entries. Its determinant is $-3$, and $(1, -1)$ gives $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = -2$.
Its determinant is 0, so $(1, -1)$ gives 0. That is semidefinite, not definite.
A negative diagonal entry gives $\mathbf{e}_2^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{e}_2 = -1$.

feedback.correct: Positive leading determinants: 2 and 3, then 4 and 8.
feedback.generic: For a symmetric $2 \times 2$ matrix, test $a > 0$ and $\det > 0$, or check both eigenvalues are positive.

explain.text: The first has $a = 2$ and $\det = 3$; the second $a = 4$ and $\det = 8$. Both pass. The others have determinants $-3$, 0 and $-3$, so some $\mathbf{x} \neq \mathbf{0}$ gives $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} \le 0$.

items.title: A hedge system
items.prose: A book is short 60 deltas and short 45 vegas. Option P adds delta 0.5 and vega 0.2 per contract. Option Q adds delta 0.25 and vega 0.4. Buying $x_P$ of P and $x_Q$ of Q must bring both to zero.
items.question: How many contracts of Q do you buy?

feedback.correct: $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.5 & 0.25 \\ 0.2 & 0.4 \end{pmatrix}$, $\det\mathbf{A} = 0.15$, and $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{A}^{-1}(60, 45) = (85, 70)$.
feedback.generic: Write delta and vega as two rows of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = (60, 45)$, with one column per option.

byKey.swapped: You swapped $b$ and $c$ in the inverse. Only $a$ and $d$ swap; $b$ and $c$ change sign.
byKey.p: You gave the number of P contracts. The question asks for Q.

items.title: What the columns reach
items.prose: Take $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 3 & 6 \end{pmatrix}$.
items.question: For which $\mathbf{b}$ does $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ have a solution? Select all that apply.

options.why: $(1, 1, 1)$ is not a multiple of $(1, 2, 3)$. You may have thought two columns reach all of space.
The last entry breaks the pattern. You checked the first two entries only.

feedback.correct: The column space is the line through $(1, 2, 3)$, and it contains $\mathbf{0}$.
feedback.generic: The second column is twice the first, so $C(\mathbf{A})$ is the line of multiples of $(1, 2, 3)$.

explain.text: Both columns are multiples of $(1, 2, 3)$, so $C(\mathbf{A})$ is that line through the origin. $(2, 4, 6)$, $\mathbf{0}$ and $(-1, -2, -3)$ lie on it. The other two do not.

items.title: Deriving the normal equations
items.prose: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has no exact solution. We want the $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ that makes $|\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{A}\hat{\mathbf{x}}|$ smallest.
items.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $\mathbf{A}\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ is the point of $C(\mathbf{A})$ closest to $\mathbf{b}$: the projection $\mathbf{p}$
$\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{A}\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ is perpendicular to every column, so $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}$
$\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{b}$: multiply out and move one term across
$\hat{\mathbf{x}} = (\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A})^{-1}\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{b}$: $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ is invertible when the columns are independent

feedback.correct: Closest point, perpendicular error, then algebra.
feedback.generic: Start from the geometry: the best fit is a projection. End by solving for $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$.

explain.text: The closest point of the column space leaves an error perpendicular to it. Writing that as $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}$ and substituting gives the normal equations. Independent columns make $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ invertible.

items.title: Naming a yield factor
items.prose: PCA on daily changes in five yields gives three loading vectors, shown here in no particular order.
items.question: Which vector is the slope factor?

options.why: Its loadings never change sign, so every yield moves together. That is the level factor.
Its sign changes twice: the ends move against the middle. That is curvature.
`eigh` lists the smallest eigenvalue first. Its order says nothing about shape.

feedback.correct: One sign change: short yields fall as long yields rise.
feedback.generic: Count the sign changes down each column: none, one or two.

explain.text: $\mathbf{w}$ runs from $-0.62$ to $0.57$ with one sign change, so it tilts the curve. $\mathbf{v}$ is level, with no change. $\mathbf{u}$, with two changes, is curvature.

items.title: How many solutions
items.prose: Solve the system $$\begin{aligned} x + 2y + z &= 3 \\ 2x + 4y + 2z &= 6 \\ x - y &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
items.question: How many solutions does it have?

options.why: You counted three equations for three unknowns. The second equation repeats the first, so the rank is 2.
You read the repeated equation as a contradiction. It agrees with the first, so the system is consistent.
A linear system never has exactly two solutions. A line of solutions holds infinitely many.

feedback.correct: Rank 2, a consistent right side, and one free variable.
feedback.generic: Find the rank, then check whether $\mathbf{b}$ is in the column space.

explain.text: Row 2 is twice row 1, so elimination leaves two pivots: rank 2 with 3 unknowns. The right side follows the same pattern, $6 = 2 \times 3$, so the system is consistent. One free variable gives a whole line of solutions.

items.title: Solving with an orthogonal matrix
items.prose: $\mathbf{Q} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.6 & -0.8 \\ 0.8 & 0.6 \end{pmatrix}$ has orthonormal columns. Solve $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{x} = (2, 1)$ without elimination.
items.question: What is $x_2$?

feedback.correct: $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{b}$, and $x_2 = \mathbf{q}_2 \cdot \mathbf{b} = -1.6 + 0.6$.
feedback.generic: For orthonormal columns $\mathbf{Q}^{-1} = \mathbf{Q}^T$, so each $x_i = \mathbf{q}_i \cdot \mathbf{b}$.

byKey.used-q: You multiplied by $\mathbf{Q}$ itself. The inverse of $\mathbf{Q}$ is $\mathbf{Q}^T$.
byKey.first: You gave $x_1$. The question asks for $x_2 = \mathbf{q}_2 \cdot \mathbf{b}$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}$, so $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{Q}^T(2, 1)$. That is $x_1 = 1.2 + 0.8 = 2$ and $x_2 = -1.6 + 0.6 = -1$. Check: $2\mathbf{q}_1 - \mathbf{q}_2 = (2, 1)$.

items.title: The largest stretch
items.prose: Take $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix}$. Its eigenvalues are 3 and 5.
items.question: What is its largest singular value $\sigma_1$? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 25 & 20 \\ 20 & 25 \end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues 45 and 5, so $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{45}$.
feedback.generic: Form $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$, find its largest eigenvalue, then take the square root.

byKey.eigenvalue: You gave the largest eigenvalue of $\mathbf{A}$. A matrix that is not symmetric can stretch further than its eigenvalues.
byKey.no-root: You gave the eigenvalue of $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$. The singular value is its square root.

explain.text: $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 25 & 20 \\ 20 & 25 \end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $45$ and $5$. So $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{45} \approx 6.7082$ and $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{5}$. Their product, 15, is $|\det\mathbf{A}|$, as it must be.

items.title: Determinant of a scaled inverse
items.prose: $\mathbf{A}$ is a $3 \times 3$ matrix with $\det\mathbf{A} = 4$.
items.question: What is $\det(2\mathbf{A}^{-1})$?

feedback.generic: Scaling a $3 \times 3$ matrix by 2 scales its determinant by $2^3$. And $\det(\mathbf{A}^{-1}) = \tfrac{1}{\det\mathbf{A}}$.

byKey.once: You scaled the determinant by 2 once. Each of the three rows carries the 2, so it is $2^3$.
byKey.no-inverse: You used $\det\mathbf{A} = 4$. The inverse has determinant $\tfrac{1}{4}$.
byKey.square: You used $2^2$, the rule for a $2 \times 2$ matrix. This one is $3 \times 3$.

explain.text: $\det(2\mathbf{A}^{-1}) = 2^3\det(\mathbf{A}^{-1}) = \tfrac{8}{4} = 2$. Volume scales by $2^3$ when every edge doubles, and the inverse undoes the factor 4.

items.title: Gram-Schmidt and R
items.prose: $\mathbf{A}$ has columns $\mathbf{a}_1 = (3, 4)$ and $\mathbf{a}_2 = (1, 2)$. Run Gram-Schmidt in that order, then write $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{R}$ with $\mathbf{R}$ upper triangular and positive on its diagonal.
items.question: Fill in $\mathbf{R}$ and $\mathbf{q}_2$.

feedback.correct: $\mathbf{q}_1 = (0.6, 0.8)$, the leftover $(-0.32, 0.24)$ has length 0.4, and $\mathbf{q}_2 = (-0.8, 0.6)$.
feedback.generic: Normalise $\mathbf{a}_1$. Subtract from $\mathbf{a}_2$ its part along $\mathbf{q}_1$, then normalise what is left.

explain.text: $\mathbf{q}_1 = \tfrac{1}{5}(3, 4)$ and $\mathbf{q}_1 \cdot \mathbf{a}_2 = 2.2$. The leftover $\mathbf{a}_2 - 2.2\,\mathbf{q}_1 = (-0.32, 0.24)$ has length 0.4. So $\mathbf{R} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 2.2 \\ 0 & 0.4 \end{pmatrix}$.

items.title: How much PC1 explains
items.prose: You run `vals, vecs = np.linalg.eigh(C)` on the covariance matrix `C` of three yields' daily changes. It returns `vals = [0.02, 0.15, 2.83]`.
items.question: What share of the total variance does the first principal component explain? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: PC1 has the largest eigenvalue, 2.83, out of a total of 3.00.
feedback.generic: Find the largest eigenvalue, then divide it by the sum of all three.

byKey.first-entry: You read the first entry. `eigh` sorts from smallest to largest, so PC1 is the last.
byKey.raw: You gave PC1's variance. Divide it by the total variance, 3.00.
byKey.two: You added the two largest. That is the share of PC1 and PC2 together.

explain.text: `eigh` returns eigenvalues in ascending order, so PC1 belongs to 2.83. The total is $0.02 + 0.15 + 2.83 = 3.00$. So PC1 explains $\tfrac{2.83}{3} \approx 94.3\%$ of the variance.

items.title: Pricing a redundant fund
items.prose: A market has three states next year. Each asset's payoff in the three states is a column.
items.question: The payoff matrix has rank 2. What fund price leaves no arbitrage?

widget.accept: Exactly £99, half a bond plus half a share

feedback.correct: The fund pays half a bond plus half a share in every state, so it costs $\tfrac12(97) + \tfrac12(101)$.
feedback.generic: Write the fund's column as a combination of the bond's and the stock's, then price it with the same weights.

byKey.worthless: You read redundant as worthless. It means the fund can be copied, so it costs what the copy costs.
byKey.no-weights: You added the two prices. The copy holds half a bond and half a share.
byKey.average: You averaged the fund's payoffs. Prices come from the copy, not from an average of payoffs.

explain.text: Solve $x_1(100, 100, 100) + x_2(80, 100, 130) = (90, 100, 115)$: $x_1 = x_2 = \tfrac12$. By the law of one price the fund costs $\tfrac12(97) + \tfrac12(101) = 99$. At any other price, buy the cheap side and sell the dear one.

items.title: Ten months of regimes
items.prose: Each month the market is calm or volatile, listed in that order. $$\mathbf{M} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.8 & 0.3 \\ 0.2 & 0.7 \end{pmatrix}$$ Column $j$ gives next month's chances from regime $j$. This month is calm, so $\mathbf{s}_0 = (1, 0)$.
items.question: What is the chance the market is calm in 10 months, the first entry of $\mathbf{M}^{10}\mathbf{s}_0$? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $\mathbf{s}_0 = (0.6, 0.4) + 0.4(1, -1)$, and the second part shrinks by 0.5 each month.
feedback.generic: Find the eigenvalues 1 and 0.5 with their eigenvectors, write $\mathbf{s}_0$ in that basis, then raise each eigenvalue to the 10th power.

byKey.steady: You gave the long-run share. After 10 months a small part of the start is still left.
byKey.nine: You used $0.5^9$. Ten months means ten multiplications by $\mathbf{M}$.
byKey.stay: You gave $0.8^{10}$, the chance of staying calm every month. The market can leave and come back.

explain.text: $\mathbf{M}$ has eigenvalue 1 with $(0.6, 0.4)$ and eigenvalue 0.5 with $(1, -1)$. So $\mathbf{M}^{10}\mathbf{s}_0 = (0.6, 0.4) + 0.4 \times 0.5^{10}(1, -1)$. The first entry is $0.6 + 0.00039 = 0.6004$.

items.title: A least squares hedge
items.prose: A book's daily P&L is `book`. Each hedge instrument has a daily P&L per unit. Holding `h` units of each makes the hedged P&L `book + X @ h`, where `X` has one column per instrument. Choose `h` so the hedged P&L has the smallest sum of squares.
items.question: Complete `hedge` with `np.linalg.lstsq`.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np

def hedge(book, instruments):
    y = np.array(book, dtype=float)
    # one column per instrument
    X = np.array(instruments, dtype=float).T
    # h minimises |y + X h|^2
    ...
    # return h as a list, rounded to 6 places
widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def hedge(book, instruments):
    y = np.array(book, dtype=float)
    # one column per instrument
    X = np.array(instruments, dtype=float).T
    # h minimises |y + X h|^2
    h = np.linalg.lstsq(X, -y, rcond=None)[0]
    # return h as a list, rounded to 6 places
    return [round(float(v), 6) for v in h]

examples.call: hedge([2 * a for a in f1], [f1])

tests.call: hedge([2 * a for a in f1], [f1])
hedge([3 * a - b for a, b in zip(f1, f2)], [f1, f2])

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests. Seven compare the positions, rounded to 6 decimal places, with math.isclose; one checks the length. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

feedback.correct: One call to `lstsq` on $-\mathbf{y}$ gives the positions that leave the smallest residual.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. A book that is exactly twice one instrument needs $-2$ units of it.

byKey.test-1: The book is twice `f1`, so the hedge is $-2$ units. Did you solve for `y` instead of `-y`?
byKey.test-2: This book is an exact mix of both instruments. Check that each instrument is its own column.
byKey.test-7: Three days, two instruments: no exact hedge exists. `lstsq` returns the least squares answer.
byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Call `np.linalg.lstsq(X, -y, rcond=None)` and take element `[0]`.

explain.text:
Minimising $|\mathbf{y} + \mathbf{X}\mathbf{h}|^2$ is least squares for $\mathbf{X}\mathbf{h} \approx -\mathbf{y}$. The residual left over is perpendicular to every instrument's column. So no further trade in any instrument can shrink it.

```python
h = np.linalg.lstsq(X, -y, rcond=None)[0]
return [round(float(v), 6) for v in h]
```

items.title: The minimum-variance portfolio
items.prompt:
Two assets have covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.04 & 0.006 \\ 0.006 & 0.09 \end{pmatrix}$. A portfolio holds weights $\mathbf{w} = (w_1, w_2)$ with $\mathbf{1}^T\mathbf{w} = 1$.

(a) Explain why the portfolio's variance is $\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w}$, and multiply it out.

(b) Minimise $\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w}$ subject to $\mathbf{1}^T\mathbf{w} = 1$ with a Lagrange multiplier. Show that $\mathbf{w}^* = \dfrac{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{1}}{\mathbf{1}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{1}}$.

(c) Compute $\mathbf{w}^*$ with the $2 \times 2$ inverse, and the portfolio's volatility.

(d) Show that $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is positive definite, and explain why that makes $\mathbf{w}^*$ the one and only minimum.
items.model:
**(a)** With returns $\mathbf{r}$ of mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}$, the portfolio return is $\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{r}$. Its variance is $E\big[(\mathbf{w}^T(\mathbf{r} - \boldsymbol{\mu}))^2\big] = \mathbf{w}^T E\big[(\mathbf{r} - \boldsymbol{\mu})(\mathbf{r} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^T\big]\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w}$. Multiplied out, it is $0.04w_1^2 + 0.012w_1w_2 + 0.09w_2^2$.

**(b)** Set $\nabla(\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w}) = \lambda\nabla(\mathbf{1}^T\mathbf{w})$. The gradient of $\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w}$ is $2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w}$, because $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is symmetric. So $2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w} = \lambda\mathbf{1}$ and $\mathbf{w} = \tfrac{\lambda}{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{1}$. The constraint $\mathbf{1}^T\mathbf{w} = 1$ fixes $\tfrac{\lambda}{2} = \dfrac{1}{\mathbf{1}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{1}}$, which gives $\mathbf{w}^*$.

**(c)** $\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = 0.0036 - 0.000036 = 0.003564$, so $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{0.003564}\begin{pmatrix} 0.09 & -0.006 \\ -0.006 & 0.04 \end{pmatrix}$. Then $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{1} = \dfrac{1}{0.003564}(0.084, 0.034)$, and the scale cancels: $\mathbf{w}^* = \tfrac{1}{0.118}(0.084, 0.034) = (0.7119, 0.2881)$. The variance is $\dfrac{1}{\mathbf{1}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{1}} = \dfrac{0.003564}{0.118} = 0.030203$, a volatility of 17.38%. That beats 20% for asset 1 alone and 18.84% for equal weights.

**(d)** The leading determinants are $0.04 > 0$ and $0.003564 > 0$, so $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is positive definite. (Its eigenvalues, 0.0393 and 0.0907, are both positive.) The Hessian of $\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w}$ is $2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, so the variance is a bowl that curves up in every direction. Along the line $w_1 + w_2 = 1$ it is an upward parabola, so its one stationary point is the only minimum.

rubric.text: Sets $2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w} = \lambda\mathbf{1}$, solves $\mathbf{w} = \tfrac{\lambda}{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{1}$, and uses the constraint to fix $\lambda$.
Computes $\mathbf{w}^* = (0.7119, 0.2881)$ and a volatility of 17.38% with the $2 \times 2$ inverse.
Shows $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is positive definite and links that to a unique minimum.

explain.text: The variance is a quadratic form, and its gradient is $2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w}$. The multiplier condition gives $\mathbf{w} \propto \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{1}$, scaled to sum to 1. A positive definite $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ makes the minimum unique.
